papers.why: Real district savings from routing optimization; the strongest operations evidence in the library.
papers.title: Optimizing schools' start time and bus routes
papers.caveat: Single district; operations outcome, not student learning.
papers.finding: Boston Public Schools used an optimization routing algorithm that saved about $5 million a year and removed 50 buses while keeping service quality.

papers.finding: On real district cases, adjusting bell times with routing cut deadhead travel 15% to 55%, averaging 20% to 30%.

papers.why: Governance lesson: technically better plans still fail without community buy-in.

papers.finding: Routing algorithm cut the Boston bus fleet 7%; a start-time plan that would have saved another $12 million and moved most high schools to 8 a.m. or later was dropped after strong community opposition because 85% of schools' times would change.

children.name: Transportation
children.blurb: Transportation planning in schools uses optimization tools to route buses and set bell times more efficiently than manual work, which can cut fleet size and empty bus travel.

children.name: Scheduling and Staffing
children.blurb: Scheduling and staffing uses software to solve the hard puzzle of fitting student course requests, teacher assignments, rooms and required courses into a master schedule, and to match substitutes to open positions.

children.name: Food Service
children.blurb: Nutrition management software can forecast how much food a school should prepare by drawing on past participation, menus, weather, and school events, and it can help draft menus that meet federal nutrition requirements.

children.name: Operations Data and Privacy
children.blurb: Operations systems such as transportation, food service and health records hold sensitive student information, and every tool that touches that data needs the same privacy protections as classroom tools.

children.name: Emergency Operations
children.blurb: Emergency operations in a school district use forecasting tools to anticipate problems like unsafe roads, while the decision to close or delay school stays with the superintendent or a designated leader.

children.name: Facilities and Energy
children.blurb: AI in school facilities and energy work means using software to predict equipment failures, sort maintenance requests by urgency, adjust heating, cooling and lighting to match occupancy, and manage facility rentals.

children.name: Budget and Enrollment Forecasting
children.blurb: Budget and enrollment forecasting uses models, often aided by AI, to predict how many students will enroll in each school and grade, because funding usually follows students.

children.name: Grants
children.blurb: AI can help school staff find grant opportunities and draft parts of applications, but every fact, figure, and claim must be verified against the district's own data and original sources.

children.name: Purchasing and Business Operations
children.blurb: Purchasing and business operations in a school district can use automation to match invoices to purchase orders and flag discrepancies, while staff review exceptions and approve payments.

children.name: Technology Operations
children.blurb: Technology operations in a school district covers the everyday systems that keep devices, networks, and data working: an IT help desk that answers common questions at any hour while sending complex problems to a person, inventory tools that track devices and predict replacements, and phishing training that teaches staff to spot attacks.

children.name: Records, Minutes, and Policy
children.blurb: Records, minutes, and policy work in a district involves three tasks where AI tools can speed up the search and drafting stages: responding to public records requests, producing board minutes, and finding what district policy says.

children.name: Safety Technology
children.blurb: Safety technology covers the AI systems some vendors sell to schools for security, such as camera analytics and weapon detection.

children.name: Cybersecurity Beyond Phishing
children.blurb: Cybersecurity beyond phishing means treating school security as a set of basic operational protections, vendor obligations, and controls on AI tools, not just as staff awareness training.

children.name: The Staff Who Do the Work
children.blurb: Operations staff such as bus drivers, cafeteria workers, custodians, maintenance staff, and office staff hold practical knowledge that data alone does not capture, and that knowledge should shape how new tools are used.

children.name: Operations in the District AI Policy
children.blurb: A district AI policy should cover operations tools, not just classroom tools, because operations decisions such as bus routes and meal portions affect students every day.

children.name: How to Read a Savings Claim
children.blurb: A verified saving is measured against a clear baseline, over a meaningful period, and includes the costs of the new tool, while a promise is only a projection that has not been tested in the district.

sections.body: This part of school life covers the everyday machinery that keeps a district running, including transportation, scheduling, food service, facilities and energy, finance and grants, technology operations, and records and governance. The book describes AI here as a tool for optimization and forecasting, useful on complex problems like bus routing, bell times, and budget planning. The clearest example is Boston Public Schools, where an optimization system redesigned bus routes, saved about $5 million a year, and removed 50 buses while keeping service quality. The same researchers proposed changing school start times to save another $12 million and move most high schools to 8 a.m. or later. Operations is where AI can save the most money in schools, but every change touches families, staff, and students.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that tools can find better answers, and people must decide whether those answers fit the community. What works is verified savings and decisions that the people affected help shape. What does not work is the optimized plan that ignores people, such as the Boston start time plan, which was dropped after strong community opposition because 85 percent of schools' times would have changed. The rule the book holds to is that when a tool promises to save money, the district must verify the savings and ask who bears any costs. The evidence base is thin, and most ideas are sound practices rather than proven methods, with only bus routing backed by published research from real districts.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section divide the work of operations into its parts and then into the rules for doing it well. A transportation director or leader would go to Transportation, Scheduling and Staffing, and Emergency Operations for routing, bell times, and safety planning, while a facilities or finance officer would go to Facilities and Energy, Budget and Enrollment Forecasting, Grants, and Purchasing and Business Operations. Food Service, Technology Operations, and Records, Minutes, and Policy cover the remaining daily functions, and Operations Data and Privacy, Safety Technology, and Cybersecurity Beyond Phishing set the limits on data and systems. The Staff Who Do the Work and Operations in the District AI Policy connect those tools to the people and the district rules that govern them. How to Read a Savings Claim is where a teacher, leader, or parent goes to judge whether any promised saving is real and fairly shared, using the questions in Figure 19.4.
